name: Ironclad Rivet Co. Selvedge Denim Jacket
description:
A raw selvedge denim jacket in a deep indigo that fades dramatically with wear — the kind of jacket that after two years looks like a topographic map of your life. Ironclad Rivet Co. is a small Tier 2 street brand operating out of a converted print shop in the outer manufacturing belt. They produce maybe eight hundred jackets a year on vintage shuttle looms, and there's usually a wait list. The construction is old-school: bartack stitching at stress points, copper rivets, a blanket-stitch interior seam.

The jacket runs slightly boxy, in keeping with the classic trucker silhouette. It has two chest pockets and two side pockets, all functional. Mechanics, artists, musicians, and anyone who appreciates things built to last wear Ironclad. It's never been advertised. It doesn't need to be.
what_it_says: You know what you like and you're not interested in being marketed to.
story_hooks: Ironclad's head craftsperson has disappeared along with the proprietary loom settings that produce their signature weave — someone wants that pattern.
A jacket that surfaced at a Shelf pawn shop has a serial number that matches one reported stolen from a Tier 4 collector's private wardrobe.
The wait list for Ironclad jackets has become a social document — cross-referencing who's on it reveals an unexpected network of people with a shared, undisclosed connection.

physical_description.visual_profile: A classic boxy trucker silhouette in deep indigo raw selvedge denim, cut with generous ease through the shoulders and torso. The jacket reads as deliberately understated—no branding visible from a distance, but up close the construction screams quality. On-body it has the posture of something that will only look better after years of wear.
physical_description.fit: Relaxed and boxy through the chest and shoulders, with a slight taper at the waist. Sleeve length hits at the wrist with room for layering. The cut allows freedom of movement—designed for people who work with their hands.
physical_description.primary_material: Raw selvedge denim, shuttle-loom woven, deep indigo warp with natural ecru weft. Pre-washes and treatments are entirely absent—this is loom-to-body fabric.
physical_description.texture: Stiff and structured when new, with a subtle diagonal twill grain. Copper rivets at pocket corners and bartack stitching at stress points create tactile focal points. The fabric itself has a slightly nubby hand, responsive to breaking-in.
physical_description.color_scheme: Deep indigo base, fading to lighter blue and white along natural wear lines—cuffs, pocket edges, seams, hip folds. Copper rivets and cream-colored blanket-stitch visible on interior seams. No dye bleed; every fade is earned.
physical_description.closures: Five copper rivets at pocket corners, classic metal button front closure, button cuffs. All hardware is untreated copper that will patina over time.
distinctive_features: Bartack stitching at all stress points—chest pockets, armholes, side seams
Copper rivets, uncoated and designed to oxidize with wear
Blanket-stitch interior seams visible when worn open or rolled
Selvedge edges visible on cuffs and hem when rolled
Two chest pockets and two side pockets, all fully functional
No visible branding—authentication only through construction quality and selvedge edge
physical_description.tier_indicator: Tier 2 luxury-adjacent. Not corpo-austere, but signals discerning taste and disposable income. Eight-hundred pieces per year. Wait list required.
physical_description.cultural_context: Worn by mechanics, makers, artists, musicians—people who value durability and authenticity over trend. The wearer signals patience, craft literacy, and rejection of fast fashion even in 2226. In the GLMZ, this is the uniform of the intentional creator class.
physical_description.condition_typical: New: stiff and rigid, deep saturated indigo, crisp seams. Worn: progressively lighter at contact points (cuffs, hips, seat, elbows), creased where the body bends, copper rivets dulled to chocolate brown. After two years: a personalized topographic map of movement and labor.
